pitfall_name: SharedArrayBuffer blocked by missing COOP/COEP headers
what_happens: WASM threads fail to initialize; `new Worker` throws or `Atomics` operations hang indefinitely.
why: SharedArrayBuffer requires Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp headers. Without them the browser disables the API entirely, silently on some browsers, with a console warning on others.
how_discovered: Spawning WASM pthreads throws 'SharedArrayBuffer is not defined' in Chrome; the error propagates up from the thread pool init. On Firefox it may appear as an Atomics deadlock that only manifests at scale. Wastes 1–4 hours diagnosing the missing headers.
mitigation: Set both headers on every response serving the page and its module assets: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`. Use a reverse proxy or CDN that supports header injection. Avoid embedding the app in an iframe from a different origin unless that page also sets the headers.

pitfall_name: JS↔WASM memory copies on large field buffers
what_happens: Passing ProverInput objects from JS to WASM triggers a memcpy of the entire buffer into WASM linear memory on every call. On 100MB+ inputs this adds seconds of latency per proof iteration.
why: WASM linear memory is not shared with JS; the JS engine must copy the buffer into WASM's addressable space before the call and (unless you use a pre-grow strategy) back out after. Large structured inputs with nested arrays force multiple copies per object graph.
how_discovered: Profiling with Chrome DevTools Memory tab or `performance.memory` shows a spike on each `prove()` call proportional to input size, not proportional to actual arithmetic. Developers mistake it for slow field arithmetic. Typical waste: 2–6 hours before the copy is identified via flame graph.
mitigation: Use WASM-side allocation and pass a pointer+length from JS, populating the WASM memory directly with `WebAssembly.Memory.prototype.export()` Buffer and typed-array views. Alternatively, use bulk memory instructions and pre-allocated views to avoid per-call malloc inside WASM. Minimize cross-boundary calls by batching inputs.

what_happens: Prover fails to allocate memory beyond ~2–3 GB of WASM heap; `memory.grow()` returns -1 and subsequent allocations throw. Workloads that pre-load SRS or witness data exceed the ceiling silently or crash.
why: Even on 64-bit hosts, standard WASM runs in a 32-bit address space (linear memory indices are i32). The theoretical max is 4GB, but browser overhead (reserved guard pages, alignment) caps usable memory around 2–3 GB. Proving workloads with large SNARK SRS or batch proofs routinely exceed this.
how_discovered: `memory.grow()` returns -1 or a subsequent `malloc` returns 0. Browser console shows an out-of-memory message that does not specify WASM vs. tab memory. This is especially common when loading a 2GB+ Powers-of-Tau file. Takes 4–10 hours to diagnose because the browser OOM kill is not distinguishable from a JS heap OOM without inspecting WASM linear memory size.
mitigation: Use multi-file SRS splitting (load only the segment needed per circuit depth), offload witness storage to IndexedDB with streaming deserialization into WASM memory in chunks, or migrate to 64-bit WASM (WASM64 / proposal-simd) if browser support is acceptable for your timeline. For currently shipped browsers, the 4GB limit is hard.

pitfall_name: WASM SIMD generates scalar field arithmetic loops
what_happens: SIMD-enabled WASM builds show no throughput improvement over scalar builds for BN128 or Goldilocks field operations; profiling reveals the hot loop is entirely scalar despite `-msimd128` codegen flags.
why: Field arithmetic on most ZK-friendly curves does not map to available SIMD lane patterns. BN128 addition requires carry chains and modular reduction that are inherently sequential; 128-bit SIMD lanes don't naturally tile 4×32-bit field elements without costly packing/unpacking that eats the parallelism gain. SIMD helps vector polynomials and FFTs but not the per-element field ops that dominate inner proving loops.
how_discovered: Microbenchmarking shows identical throughput with and without SIMD flags on field-heavy inner loops. Disassembling the WASM binary reveals SIMD instructions appear only in FFT stages. Developers waste time tuning SIMD flags expecting 4–8x speedup. Diagnosis via `wasm-objdump --disassemble` takes 1–3 hours.
mitigation: Focus SIMD tuning on FFT/NTT kernels, polynomial interpolation, and Merkle proof verification — where vector lanes map cleanly. Accept that field arithmetic inner loops will remain scalar. Use SIMD for proof verification (many independent checks) rather than proof generation.

pitfall_name: WebGPU buffer mapping stalls the GPU command stream
what_happens: Attempting to read back proof output or intermediate witness data via `buffer.getMappedRange()` causes the GPU pipeline to stall. The stall blocks subsequent GPU work for 50–500ms, making per-iteration throughput appear far lower than GPU utilization metrics suggest.
why: WebGPU buffer mapping is synchronous on the CPU side and requires the GPU to finish all prior commands in that queue before the buffer is safe to read. The GPU command stream must flush before the CPU can access the memory. For proof outputs that require polling a GPU completion fence followed by a readback, this creates a serialization that defeats async GPU compute.
how_discovered: Chrome DevTools WebGPU inspector shows the command buffer fill then empty repeatedly. The `buffer.mapAsync` promise resolves only after the GPU finishes; profiling shows idle GPU time between map and next dispatch. This is misdiagnosed as slow kernel execution for 3–8 hours until the inspector is consulted.
mitigation: Use staging buffers (CPU-visible buffers created with `MAPPABLE` usage) to decouple GPU completion from CPU readback. Record the readback into a separate command buffer and use `onSubmittedWorkDone` to poll completion before mapping. Minimize readbacks; keep computation GPU-side as long as possible. For intermediate data, keep it on the GPU rather than ping-ponging to CPU.

pitfall_name: GPU timestamp query quantization masks short kernels
what_happens: Individual kernel execution times below ~100–500µs (depending on browser and GPU) report as 0ms. Aggregate proof-time measurements show correct totals but per-kernel breakdowns are silently quantized to zero, hiding which kernels are actually bottlenecks.
why: WebGPU timestamp queries are quantized by the underlying GPU hardware timer. Desktop NVIDIA/AMD GPUs typically quantize to 100µs increments; mobile GPUs often quantize to 500µs. Chrome also applies an additional quantization layer in the ANGLE/Vulkan translation. Short FFT kernels or small polynomial operations that complete in <100µs are recorded as taking zero time, making them appear absent from flame graphs.
how_discovered: Timestamp query timestamps for known-fast kernels (FFT butterflies, field multiplies) show zero elapsed time in the WebGPU trace. Developers suspect the kernel didn't run (correctness issue) rather than timer quantization (measurement artifact). Takes 2–4 hours to identify via known-input validation and GPU trace inspection.
mitigation: For per-kernel timing, use the GPU performance counter API (`webgpu` debug extension) or aggregate kernel runtimes by running thousands of iterations and dividing total time. Avoid drawing conclusions from single-shot kernel timestamps for operations under 1ms. Cross-validate with CPU-side `performance.now()` around the `queue.submit()` call.

pitfall_name: Browser timer resolution clamping distorts benchmark deltas
what_happens: `performance.now()` reports 5–20µs resolution on some browsers; microsecond-scale proof step comparisons show 10–30% variance between runs that is actually timer noise, not algorithmic variance.
why: Chrome on Windows has historically clamped timer resolution to ~100µs for background tabs and during certain power states (PLATFORMTICK). Safari may report sub-microsecond resolution but quantize internally to ~1µs on some hardware. Firefox uses OS-native resolution but the OS itself (Windows TSC) can have variable resolution under load. Short-duration benchmarks (<1ms per operation) are dominated by timer granularity rather than actual compute time.
how_discovered: Repeated identical proof steps show high inter-run variance (CV > 15%) despite no algorithmic changes. The variance does not correlate with input size, suggesting a measurement floor effect. Developers spend 4–8 hours suspecting JIT or GC before isolating the timer issue via `performance.now()` resolution probing and OS timer APIs.
mitigation: Run each benchmark iteration 100–1000 times and take the median, discarding the first 10 warmup iterations. Use `performance.measureUserAgentSpecificTiming()` to check browser timer granularity. For critical microbenchmarks, use `AudioContext.currentTime` (uses the high-resolution audio clock, ~1µs resolution) as a secondary timer to cross-validate `performance.now()`.

what_happens: Early proof iterations are 5–20x slower than steady-state; if the benchmark window includes warmup, average throughput is drastically underestimated. Conversely, if JIT recompiles mid-run, a mid-benchmark 2–4x speedup appears as an algorithmic improvement.
why: V8 (Chrome) and SpiderMonkey (Firefox) tier WASM compilation: tier 1 is baseline (fast compile, slow execution), tier 2 is optimizing (slow compile, fast execution). Tier 2 compilation is triggered on hot loop detection, typically after 1000–10000 iterations. On WASM this is triggered per function. The recompilation itself is not free and causes a GC-like pause mid-run. Safari's NCore uses a similar tiering model.
how_discovered: A timeline trace of a 60-second benchmark shows a 3x jump in throughput at ~t=15s that is not explained by any algorithmic change. Developers mistake this for thermal throttling reversal or a circuit switching optimization. Identified by capturing a V8.log (via `--trace-wasm` flag) showing tier-up events. Wastes 3–6 hours before diagnosis.
mitigation: Discard at minimum the first 5 seconds (or first 100 iterations, whichever is larger) of every benchmark run as warmup. For long-running proofs, ensure the measurement window is entirely in steady-state. Disable tiering for microbenchmarks using `--wasm-tiering-budget=0` in Chrome flags, or run in baseline-only mode, to get stable numbers even if slower.

pitfall_name: Cross-origin iframe isolation breaks WASM module compilation
what_happens: An app embedded in an iframe from a different origin loses SharedArrayBuffer access, loses high-resolution timers (reduced to ~1ms resolution), and may have `WebAssembly.validate()` silently return false for modules that passed in a top-level context.
why: Cross-origin iframes run in a separate browsing context group. Without matching COOP/COEP headers on the parent page, the iframe is treated as less-isolated. Browsers restrict `SharedArrayBuffer`, downgrade timers, and in some cases apply additional security restrictions to WASM module instantiation from cross-origin contexts. This is not consistent across browsers: Chrome is stricter than Firefox.
how_discovered: Proof-of-concept works in a standalone tab; fails or shows degraded performance when embedded in a partner's portal. Console may show no error, just silent fallback behavior. Timer resolution degradation shows up as measurement artifacts. Takes 2–5 hours to realize the embedding context is the root cause.
mitigation: ` attribute on the iframe and ensure the parent page sets COOP/COEP. If the parent is outside your control, use `postMessage` to communicate from the iframe to a same-origin service worker that acts as a bridge. Accept that cross-origin embedded proving will be limited until OAUTH-like isolation models are standardized.

pitfall_name: Mobile browser memory kills for WASM heaps >512MB
what_happens: Tab is killed by the OS OOM killer on mobile without any JavaScript exception. On iOS Safari, `WebAssembly.Memory` allocation can trigger `processWasKilledByWatchdog` after 30 seconds of unresponsiveness, even if memory is technically available.
why: Mobile browsers (especially Safari on iOS and Chrome on Android low-RAM devices) apply aggressive per-tab memory limits. iOS Safari limits WASM linear memory to ~512MB; Chrome Android may kill tabs at ~1–2GB total tab memory. The OS-level kill is not catchable by JavaScript. Additionally, iOS Safari's JavaScriptCore watchdog timer kills long-running synchronous WASM execution if the main thread is blocked for >30 seconds, which is common during proof generation.
how_discovered: On iOS, the tab simply disappears or Safari shows a 'WebContent was killed' message. On Android Chrome, the tab reloads without warning. No JavaScript error is thrown. The pattern is: works on desktop, fails on mobile for inputs >~256MB. 5–15 hours wasted on JavaScript error hunting before realizing it's an OS kill.
mitigation: Test on actual low-end mobile hardware, not just emulators. Keep WASM heap below 300MB on iOS; use streaming/chunked proof generation to avoid the watchdog. Break up long synchronous WASM calls into `setTimeout`-yielded chunks to keep the JS event loop responsive. Consider a WebWorker to isolate the proving computation from the main thread watchdog.

pitfall_name: Readback synchronization counted as GPU compute time
what_happens: Proof iteration throughput measurements that include end-of-iteration readback show 30–70% lower throughput than GPU utilization metrics. The GPU itself is not slow; the measurement includes a GPU-to-CPU synchronization that adds 50–500ms of blocked time.
why: Measuring time from `queue.submit()` to `buffer.mapAsync()` resolution includes GPU pipeline flush, command completion, and memory transfer. This is not compute time — it's synchronization overhead. Profiling tools that attribute wall-clock time to GPU work will misattribute this to the last kernel. Most WebGPU benchmark frameworks have this bug built in by default.
how_discovered: GPU utilization metrics from `navigator.gpu.querySamplingLocations` show 85%+ GPU usage, but `performance.now()` around the submit→readback window shows 2–5x lower throughput. Flame graph shows most time in 'GPU wait' or 'buffer map'. Developers spend 3–6 hours tuning kernel dispatch order before realizing the measurement boundary is wrong.
mitigation: Separate measurement: record `performance.now()` immediately before and after `queue.submit()` for pure dispatch time, and separately measure readback time with its own `performance.now()` boundaries. Use GPU-only metrics (utilization, SM occupancy) for GPU throughput estimates. Never include mapAsync resolution in compute throughput measurements.

pitfall_name: Safari WebGPU adapter loss on page visibility change
what_happens: After a tab is backgrounded and foregrounded, `navigator.gpu.requestAdapter()` returns a new adapter with different limits, or the existing adapter's device becomes invalid. Subsequent `queue.submit()` calls throw `OperationError`. Previously computed intermediate GPU buffers may be invalidated.
why: Safari (WebKit) implements aggressive GPU resource reclamation on tab visibility change to save power. Adapters and devices are treated as volatile resources; backgrounding the tab can trigger device loss that is not automatically recovered. Unlike desktop Chrome's robust device loss handling, Safari requires explicit `device.lost` listener re-initialization.
how_discovered: Proof generation works fine on first load; fails on the second proof iteration after switching to a different tab and back. Console shows 'GPU device lost' or silent `OperationError` on submit. The bug only manifests on Safari; Chrome and Firefox handle visibility changes gracefully. Takes 2–5 hours to diagnose because the failure is non-deterministic with respect to algorithm and deterministic with respect to browser and tab focus.
mitigation: Register a `device.lost` event listener on every WebGPU device. On device loss, pause computation, re-request the adapter and device, re-upload all buffers, and resume. Implement a visibility-change handler that proactively re-initializes the WebGPU state after 5 seconds of background. Test on Safari specifically; do not assume cross-browser device-loss behavior is equivalent.
